Death Row Inmate Christa Pike Kept Alive With Ventilator After Botched Execution as Hospital Staff Tries to 'Save' Her
More than two days after her botched execution, convicted murderer Christa Pike was alive in a Tennessee hospital.
Pike, 50, was to have been executed Wednesday night in connection with a 1995 murder. However, despite being given at least two doses of the drug Tennessee uses for lethal injections — pentobarbital — she did not die.
“Hospital staff are working to save Ms. Pike’s life and to clear the pentobarbital from her system,” her lawyers wrote in a court filing, according to The New York Times.
In a separate statement, Pike’s lawyers said she was receiving treatment for “significant injuries to both arms.”
Luke Ihnen, who represents Pike through the Federal Defender Services of Eastern Tennessee, said that “we are working closely with those closest to Christa to respect her wishes, safeguard her privacy and protect her rights as a patient during this extraordinarily difficult time.”
The emergency motion filed by Pike’s lawyers said the last they were told, Pike was “intubated, on a ventilator and remains unconscious.”
“Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms. Pike’s body,” the motion said.
“Instead of remedying this failure, TDOC elected to prepare a backup set of syringes (if they were not also prepared earlier that day) and then administered another lethal dose of pentobarbital,” the motion added. TDOC is the acronym for the Tennessee Department of Corrections.
Pike “could be heard crying, whimpering, and breathing loudly” the filing said, adding that she told corrections staff her arm “feels like it’s about to burst open.”
The motion said Tennessee committed a “manifest violation” of Pike’s constitutional rights and called its actions “reckless” and “incompetent.”
Should Pike survive, next steps are unclear, as noted by The New York Times.
Outgoing Tennessee Republican Gov. Bill Lee has halted executions in the state for now, but Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn said that if elected, she would seek to execute Pike.
Pike’s lawyers have asked Lee to allow Pike to serve a life sentence in the aftermath of the botched attempt to execute her.
May Martinez, the mother of Pike’s victim, Colleen Slemmer, who was 19 at the time she was murdered, said she felt Tennessee failed her daughter and her family, according to WJXX-TV.
“All I wanted was justice,” Martinez said.
“It’s hard. I broke down in tears,” Martinez, who witnessed the failed execution, said. “She was laying on the table, talking, still laughing, picking up her head.”
“I said, ‘I don’t agree with what you guys are doing. Now I have to worry about her being out,’” Martinez said. “And then I brought up, ‘Is she going to come back to the prison?’ ‘I don’t know what we’re doing with her yet.’ That’s the answers I got.”
“I said, ‘Here we are, 31 years, and you’re laughing in my face again,’” Martinez said. “And that’s what I feel like they did.”

Christa Pike's lawyers share big update on her condition after botched execution
Washington DC - Convicted murderer Christa Pike is unconscious and on a ventilator after a botched attempt to execute her by lethal injection, her lawyers said in a court filing Friday.
After a dramatic day of legal wrangling, prison officials in Tennessee on Wednesday injected two deadly doses of the highly toxic drug pentobarbital into Pike for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer.
But witnesses said that the 50-year-old Pike remained awake longer than expected and was later heard "loudly snoring" before an ambulance rushed her to a nearby hospital.
As of Thursday evening, "Ms. Pike remains critically ill and is being treated at a Nashville-area hospital," her lawyer Luke Ihnen wrote in a filing with a Tennessee court.
"She is intubated, on a ventilator, and remains unconscious," he added.
The lawyer said medics were "working to save Ms. Pike's life" after she arrived with both arms "swollen, burned, and blistered."
In a separate filing with a federal appeals court, Pike's legal team wrote that when the execution had gone awry, and they had asked a court to halt it, attorneys for the state argued that the department of corrections "had no obligation to render life-saving care" to Pike.
Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, who was among the witnesses, angrily told a local news outlet that the "state owes me a big apology," and that it had failed her family.
Martinez, who now lives in Florida and raised money to travel to Tennessee, told WJXX television: "All I wanted was justice."
Tennessee calls off executions after "unprecedented" botched attempt
The Tennessee Department of Corrections said earlier this week that it "followed every step of the state's lawful, established execution protocol."
But the state's Republican governor, Bill Lee, who previously denied Pike clemency, halted further executions through the rest of the year while a review is conducted.
Pike's was the second failed execution in Tennessee this year. The state halted the execution by lethal injection of Tony Carruthers in May after medical staff were unable to tap a vein.
"After having endured solitary confinement for more than 20 years and a full attempt to kill her by lethal injection, Christa has endured punishment greater than any other person in the history of the American death penalty. The governor must commute Christa's sentence now," Pike lawyer Randy Spivey said earlier this week.
Pike's lawyers had argued she should be granted clemency due to her young age and mental health issues at the time of Slemmer's killing. They also cited her history of childhood sexual assault and post-traumatic stress disorder.
"This event is the worst we've seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era," Robin Maher, the executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, told The New York Times.
"There is no precedent."
President Donald Trump questioned how an execution like Pike's could fail, telling reporters that it "shouldn't be very difficult," while UN rights chief Volker Turk urged Tennessee not to make a new attempt to execute Pike.
Had the drugs killed Pike, she would have been the first woman executed by the state in more than two centuries.
In the US, only 18 women have been executed since 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

They state that prison officials had struggled to find a vein to inject the inmate and used several needles in an attempt to execute her.
Her attorneys have described how her arms remain blistered, burnt, and swollen, with Randy Spivey stating that: 'I counted at least seven needles used in her left arm alone.
He went on to add that: 'One of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her left arm after an unsuccessful attempt.'

'We don't know at this point where we are; everything we say, I think, would be speculation.'

With Christa Pike unconscious, another execution attempt is in doubt
sources.text:
With Christa Pike unconscious, another execution attempt is in doubt
NASHVILLE, Tenn. — Christa Pike was unconscious, intubated and on a ventilator in a Nashville, Tennessee, hospital a day after surviving a botched execution attempt, her lawyers said in a court filing, raising questions about whether the state could legally try to execute her again.
As of Thursday evening, Pike, 50, was critically ill, they wrote in the Friday filing in Davidson County Chancery Court, and both of her arms were swollen, burned and blistered when she arrived at the hospital.
ADVERTISING
Her condition sets the stage for an unprecedented ethical and legal quagmire: A future attempt to execute Pike could hinge on whether she is determined to be capable of what the Supreme Court has described as a “rational understanding” of the reason she is to be put to death.
And although Gov. Bill Lee has paused executions for now, the front-runner to be elected governor next month, Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, said that she would try again to execute Pike, who was convicted of the 1995 murder of a classmate.
The family of the classmate, Colleen Slemmer, deserves “swift justice,” Blackburn said in a statement, in response to questions from The New York Times.
Friday’s disclosure about Pike’s condition is the most detailed update since she survived two rounds of pentobarbital, the drug used as part of Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol, on Wednesday evening. But it also underscored the legal and medical complexities that lie ahead for Pike, her lawyers, the doctors and nurses treating her, and her loved ones.
“Hospital staff are working to save Ms. Pike’s life and to clear the pentobarbital from her system,” the lawyers wrote in an emergency court filing. In a separate statement, they said she was also receiving treatment for “significant injuries to both arms.”
In a statement, Luke Ihnen, who represents Pike through the Federal Defender Services of Eastern Tennessee, said that “we are working closely with those closest to Christa to respect her wishes, safeguard her privacy and protect her rights as a patient during this extraordinarily difficult time.”
The lawyers’ emergency filing asked a Nashville judge to order the preservation of state prison records related to Pike’s attempted execution. The records were, they wrote, evidence of “incompetent and reckless actions.”
Among the records they sought were training and employment records of the execution team, details about medical equipment and information about any “biological or chemical residue.”
The Tennessee Department of Correction declined to comment, citing the litigation. A spokesperson for the Tennessee attorney general, Jonathan Skrmetti, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Pike’s lawyers have asked the governor to allow Pike to serve the rest of her life in prison. Lee, a Republican, has ordered an investigation into what went wrong Wednesday.
What comes next for Pike and her legal case is unclear.
Pike’s lawyers said they had not been allowed direct access to Pike and asked the Nashville judge to allow a visit. And Pike had been deeply involved in legal arguments and communications on her own behalf.
“This is an intelligent woman who knew what she wanted as far as litigation and knew what she didn’t want,” said Stephen Ferrell, with the Federal Defender Services of Eastern Tennessee. “In the hopes that she does make a recovery sufficient enough to participate in this, I would like to get her input.”
Legal and ethics experts said Pike’s treatment could qualify as cruel and unusual punishment under the Eighth Amendment. But it was also possible that her medical condition would prevent execution altogether.
John H. Blume, a law professor and director of the Cornell Death Penalty Project, said based on the Supreme Court’s prior logic, “if somebody has a significant brain injury that significantly affects their cognitive capacity, I would think that same rule would apply here.”
Austin Sarat, a law professor at Amherst College, called Pike’s case “barely charted waters.”
Two decades ago, the U.S. Supreme Court barred the execution of people with mental disabilities as a violation of the constitutional ban on cruel and unusual punishment. The court has also barred the execution of people who lack a “rational understanding” of the reason they are to be put to death.
“If you don’t understand you’re about to die and do not understand you’re about to die because the state believes you have committed murder, then you may not be executed,” said Christopher Slobogin, the director of the Criminal Justice Program at Vanderbilt University.
Pike’s medical condition also presents a difficult scenario for the medical staff working to save her life: If she recovers, Tennessee might try to kill her again.
“Professionals in healthcare are faced with difficult moral situations all the time; this is a particularly challenging one,” said Dr. Jeffrey Kahn, director of the Johns Hopkins Berman Institute of Bioethics. “I also think that they know that their job is to do the best they can for the patient in front of them and not to think about that.”

sources.news_title: Christa Pike unconscious as Tennessee execution goes awry: Lawyers
sources.text:
Convicted killer Christa Pike was left critically ill, unconscious and on life support after Tennessee's failed attempt to execute her by lethal injection, her lawyers said Friday, providing the first detailed account of the injuries she sustained.
Hospital staff were working to save Pike's life and remove the drug pentobarbital from her system, her attorneys said in an emergency motion seeking a court order requiring the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve evidence from Wednesday night's botched execution.
Pike remained in critical condition, intubated and dependent on a mechanical ventilator to breathe, her lawyers said. Two doses of pentobarbital were administered intravenously at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, the state capital.
The bungled attempt to establish intravenous lines also left both of her arms "swollen, burned and blistered," apparently because pentobarbital, a highly alkaline and caustic substance, seeped into the tissue beneath her skin, according to the court filing.
The lawyers accused Department of Correction officials of disregarding prior warnings from Pike's doctors that pre-existing medical conditions, including small veins and a blood disorder called thrombocytosis, would make placing IV lines especially difficult.
"At no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms. Pike's body," her lawyers said in a filing in the Chancery Court for Tennessee's 20th Judicial District.
Witnesses to the execution attempt could hear Pike "crying, whimpering and breathing loudly throughout the procedure," the filing said.
The filing provided the fullest picture yet of the medical consequences of an attempted execution that Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee said followed the state's established protocol.
It was the state's second botched execution this year, prompting Lee to halt any further attempts to carry out the death penalty for the rest of 2026. He also ordered an independent review of what went wrong.
Pike, 50, was convicted three decades ago of first-degree murder for her role in the torture and killing of 19-year-old vocational school classmate Colleen Slemmer at the University of Tennessee campus in Knoxville in 1995, when Pike was 18.
She had been scheduled to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than two centuries and the only person in the modern era of U.S. capital punishment to be executed in the state for a crime committed as a teenager.
Pike's then-17-year-old boyfriend was tried as an adult and convicted of murder but received a life sentence with the possibility of parole. A third schoolmate, who was 18 at the time and acted as a lookout for the other two, testified for the prosecution and received probation.
Lee earlier this week rejected a clemency petition seeking to commute Pike's death sentence to life in prison without the possibility of parole. The petition argued for leniency, in part, based on her childhood history of severe neglect, sexual abuse that included two rapes and untreated mental illness.
The clemency petition also cited evidence that Pike's mother drank heavily during pregnancy, which the petition said contributed to impaired brain development that made it difficult for Pike to control her impulses.
The U.S. Supreme Court on Wednesday lifted an 11th-hour stay of execution issued earlier that day by a federal appeals court to allow more time to consider Pike's claim that her childhood trauma had not been properly considered during sentencing.
In their filing Friday, Pike's lawyers urged the state Chancery Court to order the preservation of evidence they said would show that state prison personnel violated her constitutional rights by subjecting her to cruel and unusual punishment.

Christa Pike, a death row inmate in Tennessee, United States, remains unconscious and on a ventilator after surviving an attempted lethal injection, CNN reports.
Pike’s lawyers disclosed her condition on Friday, two days after Tennessee officials attempted to execute her with two doses of pentobarbital.
The 50-year-old inmate was taken to a hospital in the Nashville area after the execution attempt failed.
Her lawyers, Stephen Ferrell and Luke Ihnen, said she was receiving treatment for the effects of the drug and had suffered significant injuries to both arms.
“She is being treated for the serious effects of the pentobarbital administered during the execution attempt, including significant injuries to both arms,” the lawyers said in a statement.
They subsequently filed an emergency motion asking a Nashville court to order the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve evidence relating to the failed execution.
Pike had been scheduled to die by lethal injection on Wednesday at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville.
Media witnesses said she appeared to remain alive after the first dose of pentobarbital was administered and that a second dose was subsequently given.
Witnesses also reported hearing Pike breathing and snoring after the drugs had been administered.
The Tennessee Department of Correction, however, said it followed the state’s approved execution procedure.
“The Tennessee Department of Correction followed every step of the State’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office,” the department said in a statement.
The agency added that the lethal injection chemical used in the protocol had consistently been effective and that the procedure did not permit additional steps beyond those carried out.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered a third-party review of the incident and halted the state’s next scheduled execution.
Lee said the state needed to determine why the outcome differed from previous executions.
Pike’s lawyers have called for her death sentence to be commuted, arguing that she suffered severe physical trauma during the failed execution.
They had previously warned courts that Pike had difficulty with intravenous access because of her medical condition and small veins.
The failed execution has also raised questions about what happens legally when a prisoner survives after receiving lethal injection drugs.
Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a fellow Job Corps worker.
She was convicted in 1996 after being found guilty of killing Slemmer in a remote area of the University of Tennessee Agricultural campus.
Pike was 18 when she committed the crime.
Her planned execution would have made her the first woman executed by Tennessee in more than 200 years.
The case is considered unusual because previous failed lethal-injection executions in the US have generally involved authorities being unable to establish an intravenous line before administering the drugs.
Legal experts cited in US media said Pike’s case is different because the lethal drug was administered, yet she survived.
There is historical precedent for prisoners surviving failed executions and later facing another execution attempt.
In 1947, 16-year-old Willie Francis survived an electric-chair execution in Louisiana after a malfunction. The US Supreme Court later rejected his challenge to a second execution, and he was executed the following year.
In 2009, Ohio officials also failed to establish an IV line while attempting to execute Romell Broom. The Ohio Supreme Court later ruled that a second execution would not violate the US Constitution’s protection against double jeopardy.
Broom remained on death row until he died of COVID-19 in 2020.
Pike’s lawyers are now seeking to preserve evidence from Wednesday’s execution while her medical and legal future remains uncertain.
The state has not announced whether it would seek to schedule another execution after the third-party review.

sources.news_title: Christa Pike in critical condition in Nashville hospital after failed execution attempt
sources.text:
Christa Gail Pike remains in critical condition in a Nashville hospital, receiving life-saving care, following the state of Tennessee’s gruesome failed attempt to execute her on September 30. According to an emergency motion filed by her attorneys Friday in Davidson County Chancery Court, Pike is unconscious, intubated and on a ventilator, and both of her arms are swollen, burned and blistered. “Hospital staff are working to save Ms. Pike’s life and to clear the pentobarbital from her system,” the filing states.
Pike, 50, was convicted in 1996 of the January 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer, 19, a fellow student at the Knoxville Job Corps, whom she and her 17-year-old boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, lured to a park and beat and tortured to death. Pike was 18. Shipp, too young for the death penalty, received a life sentence. Pike has spent three decades in prison, more than a quarter century of it in virtual solitary confinement because she was the only woman on Tennessee’s death row.
Pike’s case has drawn international attention because of the horrific abuse she suffered as a child. She was sexually assaulted by her grandmother’s boyfriend from the ages of 2 to 5, raped at 11 by a 37-year-old neighbor and raped again at 17 by a stranger. She was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) only after she was condemned to death. None of this was presented to the jury. The victim of years of brutality became a perpetrator of brutality and then the victim of the state.
Governor Bill Lee, a Republican, has called the botched execution “deeply disturbing” and a “tragedy.” He has ordered a third-party review and called off the state’s remaining execution this year, that of Gary Wayne Sutton, scheduled for December 3. But Lee had refused Pike clemency two days before the execution, and on Thursday he stressed that “the people of Tennessee have determined that the death penalty is the appropriate penalty for the most heinous crimes in the state.” He has not responded to calls from Pike’s attorneys to commute her sentence.
Responsibility for what took place in the death chamber rests with the US Supreme Court, which stands at the head of a justice system that failed Pike. On September 29, the justices denied Pike’s request for a stay without a single noted dissent. The next morning, the 6th Circuit Court of Appeals stayed the execution to consider a claim arising from the state’s own about-face: After years of branding Pike a liar about her abuse, Tennessee conceded in August that it “does not dispute the terrible things” she suffered. Within hours, the Supreme Court’s right-wing majority vacated the stay by a 6-3 vote, so that Tennessee could carry out the killing before her death warrant expired at midnight.
Pike’s attorneys had warned the courts months earlier that a blood disorder, thrombocytosis, and her small, fragile veins would make IV access difficult and could turn the execution into torture. A court-appointed special master dismissed their concerns. “Her concerns were called ‘speculation,’” the Friday motion states. “They were laughed off, scoffed at, and dismissed.”

“She is intubated, on a ventilator, and remains unconscious,” he added.

Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, who was among the witnesses, angrily told a local news outlet that the “state owes me a big apology,” and that it had failed her family.

Members of the victim's family -- including her mother, stepfather and father -- planned to attend the execution, according to Nelsen's filing.

In a statement on the stay of execution, Pike's attorney, Ferrell, said, "The court has stayed this recognizing the serious concerns about Christa's scheduled execution."
In 1996, Pike was found guilty of first-degree murder for beating, torturing and killing Slemmer, a fellow Jobs Corps worker from Knoxville, in a remote area of the University of Tennessee Agricultural campus.
Pike, who was 18 when she committed the crime, had told a friend she planned to kill Slemmer because she "just felt mean that day" and admitted to committing the crime with her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, according to court filings. Christa Pike remains in critical condition, unconscious and on a ventilator, two days after Tennessee's attempt to execute her by lethal injection failed, according to her attorneys.
Pike's lawyers said in an emergency court filing on Friday (October 2) that she is intubated and receiving breathing assistance while hospital staff work to treat her injuries and clear the lethal drug pentobarbital from her system.
The failed execution has also raised a difficult legal question: what happens when a death-row inmate survives an execution attempt?
Tennessee administered two doses of pentobarbital during Wednesday night's execution attempt, but Pike survived. Her attorneys said she suffered significant injuries to both arms after execution personnel struggled to establish intravenous access.
According to the filing, the execution team did not realise that the IV lines had been incorrectly placed or that Pike's veins had "blown", meaning the pentobarbital was not properly entering her bloodstream.
Pike's defence lawyer Randy Spivey said the execution team worked for about an hour to administer the drugs and that he counted at least seven needles in her left arm.
Neither the initial nor backup dose resulted in her death. Pike was reportedly still snoring when the execution chamber's microphone was switched off more than an hour after the procedure began.
Pike's attorneys are seeking to have her death sentence commuted following the failed execution.
The immediate legal focus, however, is on her medical condition and preserving evidence from the execution. Her lawyers have asked a Tennessee court to order the state's Department of Correction to preserve evidence relating to what happened during the procedure.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has also halted further executions for the remainder of 2026 and ordered an independent review of the state's execution procedures.
The review could therefore play a significant role in determining what happens next, particularly given that the state has acknowledged the need to examine the circumstances surrounding the failed execution.
There is legal precedent for death-row prisoners who survive an execution attempt being subjected to another attempt, although Pike's circumstances are unusual.
CNN report stated that in 1947, 16-year-old Willie Francis survived an electrocution in Louisiana after the electric chair malfunctioned. The US Supreme Court rejected his argument that a second execution would violate constitutional protections, and Francis was subsequently executed.
The news outlet also stated that another case involved Ohio death-row inmate Romell Broom. In 2009, officials spent hours trying to establish an IV line for his lethal injection but were unable to do so. Broom later challenged another execution attempt on constitutional grounds. The Ohio Supreme Court rejected his claim in 2016, ruling that establishing an IV was a preliminary step rather than the execution itself.
Broom ultimately died in prison in 2020 while still on death row.
Pike's case differs because lethal drugs were actually administered, her attorneys and legal experts have said. Austin Sarat, an Amherst College professor who studies the death penalty, described Pike's survival after the drugs entered her system as an unprecedented situation, CNN said.
“Those cases where people survive an execution create a real dilemma for the legal system. Now what?” he said.
Pike's failed execution was the state's second botched execution this year. Lee has postponed Pike's execution and another scheduled execution and ordered an independent investigation into Tennessee's procedures.
The episode has also prompted debate over whether Tennessee should continue using single-drug lethal injections or consider alternative execution methods.
For now, Pike's immediate situation is medical rather than procedural. She remains unconscious and dependent on a ventilator while doctors treat the consequences of the failed execution.
Pike, now 50, was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, whom she killed when she was 18. She had been scheduled to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than two hundred years.
Her attorneys are now seeking commutation of the death sentence, while the state faces an independent review of how an execution that was supposed to end Pike's life instead left her critically ill in a hospital.
